'''bouquetier''' (bö-ke-tēr′; F. pron. bö-kė-tyā′), ''n.'' [F., a flower-vase, bouquet-holder, < ''bouquet'': see ''bouquet.''] A bouquet-holder, especially one designed to be carried in the hand.

'''bouquetin''' (F. pron. bö-kė-taṅ′), ''n.'' [F., earlier ''bouc-estain, bouc-d’estain'' (Cotgrave), lit. ‘wool-goat’ (''bouc'', goat; ''de'', of; ''estain'', mod. F. ''étain'', carded wool), but appar. orig. a transposition of G. ''steinbock'', D. ''steenbok'': see ''steinbok.''] The European ibex or steinbok, ''Capra ibex''; hence, a name of the rock-goats of the genus ''Ibex''.

'''bour†''', '''boure†''', ''n.'' Middle English forms of ''bower''<sup>1</sup>.

'''bourach'''<sup>1</sup>, '''bourock''' (bör′aċh, -ok), ''n.'' [Sc., also written ''bowrock, boorick'', prob. dim. of ''bour, boure'', = E. ''bower''<sup>1</sup>, q. v. Cf. ''bourach''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' An inclosure: applied to the little houses built in play by children.—'''2.''' A small cot or hut.

'''bourach'''<sup>2</sup> (bör′aċh), ''n.'' [Sc. (cf. ''borra, borradh'', a heap of stones), < Gael. ''borrach'', a projecting bank; cf. ''borra, borr'', a knob or bunch, ''borradh'', a swelling. Cf. ''bourach''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A small knoll. ''Hogg.''—'''2.''' A heap; a confused heap; a cluster, as of trees or people; a crowd.

'''bourasque''' (bö-ràsk′), ''n.'' [F. ''bourasque'', now ''bourrasque'' = It. ''borasco'', a storm, tempest, gust: see ''borasco.''] A tempest; a storm.
{{smaller block|These were members of the Helter Skelter Club, of the Wildfire Club, and other associations formed for the express purpose of getting rid of care and sobriety. Such dashers occasioned many a racket in Meg’s house and many a ''bourasque'' in Meg’s temper.
{{right|''Scott'', St. Ronan’s Well, I. 27.}}}}

'''Bourbon''' (bör′bọn), ''n.'' [< F. ''Bourbon,'' > Sp. ''Borbon,'' It. ''Borbone.''] '''1.''' A member of the last royal family of France, or of any of its branches.
{{smaller block|The family took its name from its ancient seigniory of Bourbon (now Bourbon l’Archambault, in the department of Allier), and succeeded to the throne by collateral inheritance in 1589, in the person of Henry IV. The Bourbon dynasty was deposed in 1792, and restored in 1814. The revolution of 1830 brought to the throne Louis Philippe (who was deposed in 1848), of the younger or Orleans branch, which succeeded to all the claims of the family on the extinction of the elder branch in 1883. A line of Bourbon sovereigns has reigned in Spain (with two interruptions) since 1700, and a branch of this line held the throne of Naples or the Two Sicilies from 1735 to 1861.}}
'''2.''' One who, as was said of the Bourbons, “forgets nothing and learns nothing”; hence, in ''U. S. politics,'' an extreme conservative; especially, one who is behind the time and is opposed to all progress: originally applied to certain members of the Democratic party.—'''3.''' [''l. c.''] A kind of whisky made of wheat or Indian corn: originally limited to the corn-whisky made in Bourbon county, Kentucky.

'''Bourbonian''' (bör-bō′ni-an), ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the family or dynasties of the Bourbons.

'''Bourbonism''' (bör′bọn-izm), ''n.'' [< ''Bourbon'' + ''-ism''; = F. ''Bourbonisme.''] '''1.''' The opinions of those who adhere to the house of Bourbon; legitimism.—'''2.''' In ''U. S. politics,'' obstinate conservatism; opposition to progress.

'''Bourbonist''' (bör′bọn-ist), ''n.'' [< ''Bourbon'' + ''-ist''; = F. ''Bourboniste.''] One who supports the claims of the members of the house of Bourbon to the thrones they held; specifically, a supporter of the claims of the members of this

'''Bourbon palm.''' See ''palm''.

'''bourd<sup>1</sup>†''' (börd), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''boward'', ''boorde'', < ME. ''boorde'', ''bourde'', ''borde'', ''burde'' = MD. ''boerde'', D. ''boert'' = OFries. ''bord'' = LG. ''boert'', a jest, < OF. ''bourde'', ''borde'', mockery, banter, jest, F. ''bourde'', bouncer, humbug, = Pr. ''borda'', a jest, a cheat, a lie; cf. Bret. ''bourd'', a jest (prob. < F.), Gael. ''buirte'', a gibe, taunt, ''burt'', ''buirt'', mockery, = Ir. ''buirt'', a gibe, taunt. Origin and relations uncertain.] '''1.''' A jest; a joke; fun.
{{smaller block|Whether our maister speake earnest or ''borde''.
{{right|''Udall'', Roister Doister, i. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Gramercy, Borrill, for thy company,
For all thy jests, and all thy merry ''bourds''.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Shepherd’s Garland, p. 53.}}}}
'''2.''' Mockery; scoffing.

'''bourd<sup>1</sup>†''' (börd), ''v.'' [< ME. ''bourden'', < OF. ''bourder'', sport; from the noun: see ''bourd''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To jest; joke; say things in jest.
{{smaller block|My wit is greet, though that I ''bourde'' and pleye.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Pardoner’s Tale, l. 316.}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make game of.
{{smaller block|<poem>Shew
But any least aversion in your look
To him that ''bourds'' you next, and your throat opens.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, i. 1.}}}}

'''bourg<sup>1</sup>''' (börg), ''n.''   [F., < ML. ''burgus'', < OHG. MHG. ''burc'', G. ''burg'' = E. ''borough''<sup>1</sup>, q. v. Cf. ''burg''<sup>1</sup>, ''burgh.'']   A town; a borough: chiefly with reference to French towns. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Ye think the rustic cackle of your ''bourg''
The murmur of the world!</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}

'''Bourg<sup>2</sup>''' (börg), ''n.'' A name given to the red wine of a large district in France in the department of Gironde, on the north bank of the Dordogne.

'''bourgade''' (bör-gäd′), ''n.''   [F., < ''bourg'', a town, market-town: see ''bourg''<sup>1</sup>.]   A straggling village; a small French or Swiss market-town.
{{smaller block|The canton consists only of villages and little towns or ''bourgades.'' {{right|''J. Adams'', Works, IV. 32.}}}}

'''bourgeois<sup>1</sup>''' (bör-zhwo′), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [F., mod. form of OF. ''burgeis'', a citizen, > E. ''burgess'', q. v.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' In France, a citizen; a burgher; a man of middle rank.—'''2.''' A small French coin of the fourteenth century. {{smaller|The ''bourgeois simple'' was worth about a cent and a half, the ''bourgeois fort'' twice as much.}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Belonging to or consisting of tradespeople or citizens of middle rank: as, ''bourgeois'' surroundings; the ''bourgeois'' class of France. Hence—'''2.''' Wanting in dignity or refinement; common; mean.
{{smaller block|We have no word in English that will exactly define this want of propriety in diction. Vulgar is too strong, and commonplace too weak. Perhaps ''bourgeois'' comes as near as any. {{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 26.}}}}

The F. name for this type is ''gaillarde'': see ''gailliarde, galliard''.]   A size of printing-type measuring about 100 lines to the foot, next larger than brevier and smaller than long-primer.
{{c|This line is printed in ''bourgeois''.}}

{{smaller block|There is no ''bourgeoisie'' to speak of; immediately after the aristocracy come the poor people, who are very poor indeed. {{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Trans. Sketches, p. 263.}}}}

'''bourgeon''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''burgeon''.

'''bourgignot, bourginot''', ''n.'' Variants of ''burganet''.

'''Bourguignon''' (F. pron. bör-gē-nyôṅ′), ''n.''   [F., < ''Bourgogne'', Burgundy.]   A native or an inhabitant of Burgundy; a Burgundian.

'''Bourignian''' (bö-rin′yan), ''a.'' Pertaining to the Bourignonists or to their doctrines.

'''Bourignonist''' (bö-rin′yon-ist), ''n.'' One of a sect founded by Antoinette Bourignon (1616–80), a religious enthusiast who assumed the Augustinian habit, and traveled in France, Holland, England, and Scotland. {{smaller|She maintained that Christianity does not consist in faith and practice, but in inward feeling and supernatural impulse.}}

'''bourn<sup>1</sup>, bourne<sup>1</sup>''' (bōrn), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''boorne, borne'', < ME. ''bourne, borne'', var. of earlier ''burne'' (whence the reg. northern form ''burn''<sup>2</sup>, q. v.), < AS. ''burne'', ''burna'', a stream: see ''burn''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. E. ''mourn'', < AS. ''murnan''.]   A stream; a brook: same as ''burn''<sup>2</sup>.
{{smaller block|Come o’er the ''bourn'', Bessy, to me.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 6 (song).}}}}
{{smaller block|[The word occurs in various place-names in Great Britain, as ''Bournemouth'' (that is, mouth of the burn or rivulet), ''Westbourne'', etc.]}}

'''bourn<sup>2</sup>, bourne<sup>2</sup>''' (bōrn or börn), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''borne''; < F. ''borne'', formerly also ''bourne'', a var. of OF. ''bodne'', ''bonne'', a limit, bound, boundary, > E. ''bound''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.]   A bound; limit; destination; goal: as, “beyond the ''bourn'' of sunset,” ''Tennyson'', Princess, Conclusion.
{{smaller block|<poem>The undiscovered country, from whose ''bourn''
No traveller returns. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 1.}}</poem>
There at last it lay, the ''bourn'' of my long and weary pilgrimage, realizing the plans and hopes of many and many a year.
{{right|''R. F. Burton'', El-Medinah, p. 389.}}}}

'''bourn<sup>3</sup>, bourne<sup>3</sup>''' (bōrn), ''v. t.'' See ''bone''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bournless''' (bōrn′- or börn′les), ''a.''   [< ''bourn''<sup>2</sup> + ''-less''.]   Having no bourn or limit. [Rare.]

'''bournonite''' (bör′nọ-nīt), ''n.''   [After Count de ''Bournon'', a French mineralogist (1751–1825).]   A sulphid of antimony, lead, and copper, of a steel-gray color and brilliant metallic luster, found in the Harz mountains, Cornwall, and Mexico. {{smaller|''Wheel-ore'' is a variety which owes its name to the form of the twin crystals, resembling a cog-wheel. Also called ''endellionite''.}}

'''bournous''' (bör-nös′), ''n.'' A French spelling of ''burnoose''.

'''bourock,''' ''n.'' See ''bourach''<sup>1</sup>.

'''bourran,''' ''n.'' See ''buran.''

'''bourrée''' (bö-rā′), ''n.''   [F.: see ''boree.'']   '''1.''' A lively dance, originating either in Auvergne or in Biscay.—'''2.''' A musical composition in which the strict rhythm and cheerful character of such a dance are embodied. {{smaller|It is usually written in duple rhythm, the phrases being two measures long, beginning}} {{img float|file=century v01 p0669 c3f1.png|width=185px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Bourrelet in head-dress of Queen Isabeau of Bavaria; about 1395. (From Viollet-le-Duc’s “Dict. du Mobilier français.”)}}}}
{{smaller|with the last half of the up-beat. It was much used as one member of the old-fashioned ''suite,'' and is still popular as a form of composition. It is allied to the ''gavot.''}}

'''bourrelet''' (bör-lā′), ''n.''   [F.: see ''burlet.'']   '''1.''' The stuffed roll (see ''burlet'') which formed a part of female head-dress in the fourteenth century.—'''2.''' In ''milit. costume,'' a wreath or turban of stuff, worn upon the helmet.—'''3.''' In ''her.'' See ''tortil.''

'''bourse''' (börs), ''n.''   [F., a purse, bursary, an exchange, < OF. ''borse,'' < ML. ''bursa,'' a purse, bag, etc.: see ''burse, purse.'']   '''1.''' A stock exchange; specifically, the stock exchange of Paris, and hence used of continental European exchanges in general.

{{smaller block|Fraternities and companies I approve of, as merchants’ ''bourses'', colleges of druggists, physicians, musicians, etc.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., To the Reader, p. 65.}}}}
'''2†.''' The bag of a wig. See ''bag''<sup>1</sup>, 3.

'''bour-tree''' (bör′trē), ''n.''   [Sc., also spelled ''burtree'', ''bore-tree'', and ''boun-tree'', and formerly ''burttree'', < ME. ''burtre'', < ''bur-'' (uncertain, but not, as supposed by some, < ''bore''<sup>1</sup>, as if from the use of elder-twigs, with the pith removed, as tubes; cf. Sc. ''bourtree-'', ''bountry-gun'', an air-gun of elder) + ''tree''.]   A Scotch name of the elder-tree, ''Sambucus nigra''.—{{smaller|'''Bourtree-gun''', a pop-gun or bean-shooter made of the wood of the bour-tree after the pith has been removed.}}

'''bousa''' (bö′sä), ''n.'' Same as ''boza''.

''bousing''.   [Also written ''bowse'', ''bouze'', and also, repr. the now most common though dial. pron., ''boose'', ''booze''; early mod. E. ''bouse'', ''bowse'', < ME. ''bousen'' (rare), appar. < MD. ''būsen'', later ''buisen'', ''buysen'' = G. ''bausen'', drink, guzzle; cf. MD. ''buise'', a large drinking-vessel, appar. identical with D.
